newsitem.title: UK: Megalomedia focuses on acquiring profitable firms.
newsitem.headline: Megalomedia focuses on acquiring profitable firms.

text.p: Megalomedia Plc, founded a year ago by advertising guru Maurice Saatchi, continues to seek acquisitions, but chief executive Chris Parker said it is focusing on acquiring larger, profit-making businesses rather than start-up companies in new media fields.

"We don't want too many more of the minority, blue sky stakes," Parker told Reuters in an interview. "We don't want too many of them, because you can spend just as much time and energy on a little one as a big one. We've got three (minority stakes). We might take it up to five."

"What we would like is another two or three more substantial businesses -- a million to 3 million in profits," Parker said. He said Megalomedia's main thrust is to make such acquisitions over the next six months.

A company posting pre-tax profits of one million to three million pounds would command an acquisition price of eight million to 50 million pounds. "Fifty million is clearly at the upper end of what we could afford," Parker said.
Asked if Megalomedia is currently engaged in any active talks, he said, "Yes, loads. Well six or eight."
Megalomedia has used its controlling stake in three established, profit-making companies to fund minority investment in start-up new media ventures.

The established businesses include FrameStore, specialising in digital special visual effects and computer animation for film and television, Forward Publishing, a contract magazine publisher for corporate clients, and Graduate Appointments, a recruiting firm previously owned by Maurice Saatchi's wife, Josephine.

Framestore is currently seeking acquisitions, especially in the computer graphics and animation areas, and Megalomedia would also like to acquire a business in traditional informational publishing, Parker said.

The Saatchi family owns about 30 percent of Megalomedia's stock and Maurice Saatchi is non-executive chairman. But while Parker talks to Saatchi two or three times a week and the Saatchi reputation helps open doors for Megalomedia, Parker said there are no links with Saatchi's M & C Saatchi advertising agency.
"They do a lot of work with Forward Publishing and very little work with any of the others," Parker said.
There are no plans to marry the two companies, either. "Obviously we discussed at the beginning bringing the two companies together," Parker said.

But M & C Saatchi, born after Saatchi was ousted from the advertising agency he had founded and chaired after a bruising battle instigated by a U.S.-based shareholder, decided against being part of a publicly held company.
"For very obvious reasons the last thing they wanted to do was rush back into a public company," Parker said.
Megalomedia, meanwhile, opted for public ownership to give it access to capital and to foster its acquisition interests. It is listed on London's Alternative Investment Market.

Acquisitions to date include minority stakes in Webmedia Group Ltd, a Website design and Website name registration company, Cybercafe Ltd, operator of Internet cafes, and Multimedia Corp Plc, a publisher of CD-ROMs.
But despite the press attention that new media ventures command, Megalomedia's greatest growth potential lies with its established businesses.

Multimedia, like other CD-ROM publishers, has been hit by sluggish sales in the key U.S. market, where computer users are turning to the Internet rather than buying CD-ROMs. Parker said the company "...is in a bit of wait and see mode."

Multimedia's image software business, which digitizes photos and sets up electronic photo libraries, is more promising. "If they could get a tie-up with a multi-national company that could give them access to distribution, they could go gangbusters," Parker said.
Webmedia is involved in the fast-growing corporate Website design field, which Parker said he expects will evolve much like the traditional contract publishing field.
"There are no contract publishers that are huge businesses, but there are contract publishers that make a couple million pounds a year in profits," he said.
